did_you_know.text: The chapter presents Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters: Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem. Both are described as belonging to the LORD and having sons and daughters.
Oholah, representing Samaria, is described as relying on Assyria and being attracted to its leaders and warriors.
According to the chapter, Samaria was handed over to the Assyrians: her sons and daughters were taken away, and she herself was killed by the sword, becoming an object lesson and a punishment.
Oholibah, representing Jerusalem, saw what happened to her sister Samaria, but according to the prophecy, she became even more corrupt in her ways.
The chapter depicts the Chaldean men of Babylon as figures painted on a wall, dressed in military clothing and having the appearance of men from their homeland.
After seeing the Babylonian figures, Oholibah sent messengers to them; this portrays Jerusalem turning to Babylon in the allegory of political and religious adultery.
The punishment for Oholibah comes precisely from the nations she once trusted: the Babylonians, the Chaldeans, and the Assyrians are summoned against her.
Jerusalem is commanded to drink the “cup of your sister Samaria”—an image of a deep, bitter, shameful punishment that brings desolation.
Among the sins of the two kingdoms, the chapter lists idolatry, bloodshed, sacrificing children to idols, defiling the temple, and profaning the Sabbaths.
The chapter concludes that the punishment is also meant to bear the guilt of their idolatry and to bring the people to acknowledge: “Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.”
